stem: What do the options in ss -tln stand for?

options.text: TCP sockets, in all states, with the timers shown on each
options.why: -l limits the list to listening sockets; timers are -o.

options.text: TCP sockets, listening only, shown as numbers not names
Traffic counters, taken over the last number of minutes
options.why: ss shows sockets, not traffic counters.

options.text: Terminal output, long format, with no header line at the top
options.why: The letters are t for TCP, l for listening and n for numeric.

explain: ss -tln: t = TCP, l = listening, n = numeric ports and addresses. Add -p (with privileges) to see which process owns each socket.

stem: A database is used only by a program on the same machine. Where should it listen to limit exposure?

options.why: That accepts connections on every interface, including from the network.
A service binds to its own addresses, not to the router's.
That is the broadcast address; a service does not listen there.

explain: Binding to the loopback address is part of hardening: a service nobody remote needs should not be reachable remotely.

stem: Which command lists current TCP connections rather than listeners?

options.why: -l limits the list to listening sockets.
That shows addresses on the interfaces.
ping tests reachability; it does not list connections.

explain: Without -l, ss shows sockets that are connected. Together with -l it can show both views of the same machine.
